newsitem.title: UK: New Labour era, new generation under PM Blair.
newsitem.headline: New Labour era, new generation under PM Blair.

text.p: New Labour, new dawn, new generation.

As Tony Blair entered Downing Street under a cloudless sky on Friday, there was a feeling in the air among hundreds of cheering supporters, and millions watching television at home, that he represented far more than a change of government.
A Labour landslide in Thursday's British elections swept away 18 years of rule by a Conservative Party seen as tired, out of touch and based on old-fashioned tenets of class and privilege.

Over the past three years Blair, 43, has undertaken a root-and-branch revamp of his Labour Party, discarding socialist shibboleths that had dogged the party's electoral hopes and giving "New Labour" a gloss that attracted voters in droves.

Blair is the youngest British prime minister this century but, more importantly, he is the first premier to know nothing of World War Two and its privations. As he himself says, he represents the rock n' roll generation of the 1960s. Blair was aware of the significance of the moment.
"A new dawn has broken, has it not? And it is wonderful," Blair earlier told a sea of delirious supporters as the sun rose over the Royal Festival Hall on the banks of the River Thames.
"Today on the eve of this new millennium the British people have ushered in this new era of politics."

Many in the crowds lining the streets in central London on Friday to catch a glimpse of Blair were not born when Labour last won an election in 1974. He was a student at Oxford University at the time, playing in a rock band, Ugly Rumours.
Unlike Conservative John Major and his predecessor as prime minister, Margaret Thatcher, Blair remains in closer touch with modern life through his young family -- Euan, 13, Nicholas and Kathryn.

He and wife Cherie hugged the children openly on the steps of 10, Downing Street, something unthinkable in the days of Iron Lady Thatcher. Cherie, a successful lawyer who earns far more than her husband, is the first working mother in Downing Street.
Crowds of supporters, many waving Union Jack flags and some in tears, strained forward to touch Labour's messiah.

"Tony, Tony, Tony," they chanted, and "Labour's coming home," mimicking a song popular in the European soccer championship. The scene was a mixture of school sports day and a political rally -- children were everywhere.
The flak-jacketed policemen guarding Blair smiled, stepped back and let it all happen.
